items.title: Grammar essentials — tenses, articles, prepositions, agreement
items.body:
The **20-mark grammar MCQ** section (Item 09) rewards a few reliable rules.

**Tenses (time + link):**
- 'since + point' / 'for + period' → present perfect (*has lived since 2015 / for ten years*).
- Action finished before another past action → past perfect (*had left before I arrived*).

**Articles by SOUND, not spelling:**
- a university, a European (consonant /y/ sound); an hour, an honest man (silent h); an MP (vowel sound of 'em').
- 'the' for something specific/unique (*the sun, the Prime Minister*).

**Prepositions (fixed pairs):**

| Word | Prep | Word | Prep |
|---|---|---|---|
| accused | of | married | to |
| charged | with | good | at |
| blamed | for | different | from |

**Subject–verb agreement:**
- 'One of the + plural' → singular verb (*one of the boys **is***).
- Ignore words between the subject and verb.
keyPoints: 'since + point' and 'for + period' take the present perfect (has/have + V3).
Choose a/an by sound: an hour, a university, an MP.
Use 'the' for specific or unique things.
Fixed pairs: accused of, charged with, married to, good at, different from.
'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb; ignore words between subject and verb.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Grammar (Item 09); SSC-standard rules.

items.title: Voice, narration and sentence transformation — conversion rules
items.body:
**Active → Passive:** keep the tense, swap subject/object, add 'by'. Use the right form of 'be' + past participle.

| Active tense | Passive |
|---|---|
| present simple (writes) | is/are written |
| past simple (wrote) | was/were written |
| present perfect (has written) | has/have been written |
| modal (must write) | must be written |

**Direct → Indirect (narration):** back-shift the tense and change time/pronoun words.
- will→would, can→could, may→might; is→was; go→went.
- now→then, today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there.
- Statements use 'that'; questions use 'asked' + (wh-word / if-whether) with normal word order; requests use 'requested + object + to-infinitive'.

**Common transformations:**
- too ... to = so ... that + cannot.
- No sooner ... **than** ...; Hardly ... **when** ...
- 'One of the largest cities' (superlative) = 'Very few cities are as large as ...' (positive).
keyPoints: Passive = correct form of 'be' + past participle, keeping the original tense.
Narration back-shift: will→would, can→could, is→was; now→then, tomorrow→the next day.
Reported questions use 'asked' + wh-/if-whether with statement word order.
'too ... to' = 'so ... that + cannot'.
Correlatives: 'No sooner ... than', 'Hardly ... when'.

items.title: Vocabulary & word-building — synonyms, one-word, affixes, confusables
items.body:
Several MCQ areas reward a strong vocabulary and word-building sense.

**Synonyms/Antonyms:** learn word + opposite together (benevolent↔malevolent, candid↔evasive, abundant↔scarce).

**One-word substitution:** replace a phrase with one precise term — *bureaucracy* (rule by officials), *illiterate* (cannot read/write), *aviary* (place for birds), *polyglot* (knows many languages).

**Affixes (assimilation):** negative 'in-' becomes **il-** before l (illegal), **ir-** before r (irregular), **im-** before m/p (impossible). Suffix '-less' = without (fearless); '-ful' = full of (careful).

**Idioms:** figurative, not literal — *burn the midnight oil* (study late), *bury the hatchet* (make peace), *at the eleventh hour* (last moment).

**Confusables/homophones:** affect (verb) vs effect (noun); stationary (still) vs stationery (paper); their/there/they're; principal (head) vs principle (rule).

**Administrative glossary:** agenda (items to discuss), minutes (record after), quorum (minimum members), memorandum (note of terms).
keyPoints: Learn synonym/antonym pairs together (benevolent↔malevolent, abundant↔scarce).
One-word substitutions: bureaucracy, illiterate, aviary, polyglot.
Negative 'in-' assimilates: il- before l, ir- before r, im- before m/p.
Idioms are figurative: burn the midnight oil, bury the hatchet, at the eleventh hour.
Confusables: affect(v)/effect(n), stationary/stationery, principal/principle.
Admin terms: agenda vs minutes vs quorum vs memorandum.
items.source: SSC-standard English vocabulary (Items 08-14 of grammar list).

items.title: Composition I — formal letter & press release/appeal
items.body:
**Formal letter (Item 02, ~100 words, 10 marks)** — an opinion on an office matter/issue.

Layout: sender's address + date → receiver's designation/address → **Subject** → salutation (*Dear Sir/Madam*) → ¶1 purpose → ¶2 details/opinion → ¶3 courteous request/close → **Yours faithfully** → name.
- Tone: polite, formal, no contractions; purpose in the first line; one idea per paragraph.

**Press release / Appeal (Item 03, ~100 words, 10 marks)** — on a recent concern/problem/disaster/rumour.

Layout: organisation name + **PRESS RELEASE / APPEAL** label → headline → dateline (place, date) → body (most important fact first — *inverted pyramid*) → a spokesperson quote / contact.
- For an appeal: name the cause and the exact help needed; keep it factual and quotable.
keyPoints: Formal letter (~100 words, 10 marks): address, date, Subject, salutation, purpose→details→request, 'Yours faithfully'.
Letter tone is polite and formal with the purpose stated in the first line.
Press release/appeal (~100 words, 10 marks): label + headline + dateline + inverted-pyramid facts + quote/contact.
An appeal must name the cause and the specific help needed.
Both are factual and impersonal — no slang or contractions.

items.title: Composition II — report, visual information & formal speech
items.body:
**Report writing (Item 04, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — of a function/event/field trip/survey.
- Heading + by-line → opening with the **5 Ws** (what, when, where, who, why) → factual details in order → outcome.
- Style: **third person, past tense, objective** — no personal feelings.

**Writing on visual information (Item 05, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — a graph/table/flow-chart/statistics.
- State what the visual shows (title, units, period) → give the **main trend** → key figures and comparisons → notable exceptions.
- **Describe, do not interpret**; no opinions. Use comparison language (higher than, doubled, the largest).

**Formal speech (Item 06, ~150 words, 15 marks)** — inauguration/seminar/ceremony.
- Greeting to audience/dignitaries → introduce the topic → 2-3 points with examples → an appeal → close + thanks.
- Use direct address ('respected guests'), short sentences, a memorable ending.
keyPoints: Report (~150 words, 15 marks): heading + by-line + 5 Ws; third person, past tense, objective.
Visual information (~150 words, 15 marks): state what it shows, give the main trend, key figures — describe, don't interpret.
Use comparison language for visuals (higher than, doubled, the largest); no opinions.
Formal speech (~150 words, 15 marks): greeting, topic, 2-3 points, appeal, close with thanks.
Speech uses direct address and short, memorable sentences.
